newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Poland warns against big power NATO-Russia deal.
newsitem.headline: Poland warns against big power NATO-Russia deal.

text.p: Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, visiting NATO to push Warsaw's membership plans, warned the major Western powers on Friday not to cut a deal with Russia over the heads of other countries.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said earlier on Friday she had made important progress on a deal with Russia which is designed to overcome Moscow's hostility to NATO enlargement.

But Cimoszewicz echoed fears, both in Eastern Europe and among some NATO allies, that the United States and other major countries might ignore their concerns and push on with a 19th century-style great power carve-up with Russia.

Any deal with Moscow, he told the alliance, should be "transparent" and take into account the concerns of non-members. Poland would not accept any deal which would make it a "second-class" member of the Western alliance when it joins.

"In a system of cooperative security, there is no place for geopolitics, spheres of influence, secret protocols or concerts of great powers," Cimoszewicz told ambassadors from the 16 North Atlantic Treaty Organisation nations in Brussels.
"We trust that our NATO partners share this view. We hope so does Russia."
At a Madrid summit in July, NATO will invite a number of Eastern European countries - widely expected to include Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic -- to join the alliance.
Moscow, fearing Europe's security balance will be upset, says the alliance's expansion into what was once Soviet-dominated Eastern Europe represents a threat to its security.

NATO insists that Moscow has no veto over its plans and that enlargement will go ahead, but is also trying to appease Russia with an accord that would build a new security relationship with its former enemy.

A recent French suggestion for a five-nation summit of major powers to discuss the issue annoyed many smaller alliance countries, which felt left out, and made Eastern European nations like Poland uneasy.

Cimoszewicz said NATO's dialogue with Moscow should in no way limit the freedom of other countries to shape relations with the alliance as they wish. He said he had sensed support for his approach during the meeting with NATO ambassadors.

Poland, he said, backed NATO's assertion that there was no question of stationing nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states -- a pledge that is part of the package designed to reassure Russia that NATO poses no threat.
"We neither see the need to have them on our soil nor have (we) any intention to change our position in the future," he said.
"We strongly oppose, however, any accords which would make us second-class NATO members."

Following visits by Albright and other Western leaders to Moscow, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov is to visit Brussels on Sunday for talks with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana. Solana has been charged with negotiating the terms of a new relationship between Russia and the alliance.
